rule_text: All items must be written in third person. Avoid use of 'I', 'us', 'our', 'we', 'my'. Replace with the organization name or neutral phrasing.
All submissions must be concise and clear. This is not the space to be witty or poetic.
Never use exclamation marks in headlines. Avoid them in body text. Use a professional, neutral tone.
All event-related listings must include the time, date, and location of the event. If an activity is not free, a price must be included.

When a source pairs a relative date such as 'today' or 'tomorrow' with a specific calendar date, retain both in the edited copy. Never replace or remove the calendar date. Write the relative reference followed by the date, such as 'today, Aug. 24,' so the item remains accurate after publication.
Embed hyperlinks in meaningful anchor text rather than displaying raw URLs. Use descriptive link text like 'Learn more', 'Register', 'Apply now'.

Use AP style for dates. Abbreviate Jan., Feb., Aug., Sept., Oct., Nov. and Dec. only when used with a specific date. Never abbreviate March, April, May, June or July. When a month appears without a specific date, spell out the full month name. Use numerals for dates (Jan. 5, not January fifth). When a month-and-day date appears mid-sentence, place a comma after the date if the sentence continues: 'The conference runs Monday, Oct. 31, and Tuesday, Nov. 1.' Apply the comma to every date in a range or sequence.

Use AP style for times: lowercase a.m. and p.m. with periods. Use noon and midnight instead of 12 p.m. and 12 a.m. Use figures: 1 p.m., 3:30 p.m. Use a hyphen for same-period time ranges: '3-4 p.m.' Use 'to' instead of a hyphen when a range crosses a.m. and p.m.: '11 a.m. to 2 p.m.' Use 'from' only when the sentence grammar requires a from/to construction. Avoid 'o'clock'. Remove redundant time phrases such as 'this morning' or 'tonight'.
Lengthy submissions should display with a few sentences in the newsletter and a link to a website containing the entire message. UCM reserves the right to trim lengthy submissions.
Items generally run once. They can run twice if there is an RSVP or registration component.
Items running more than once should not be resubmitted with altered text unless the original has an error.
Announcements should be chronological, with more important items at the top (e.g., university-wide announcements, urgent notices).
All submissions must be affiliated with the University of Idaho.
Thesis defenses are not included in the newsletter.
Sports competitions outside the Moscow-Pullman, Lewiston-Clarkston area are not included.
Limited-audience application deadlines and items intended for a small subset of the audience should be handled through other means.
Body text must be exactly one paragraph. Do not use bullet points, numbered lists, or multiple paragraphs.
Do not use bold, italics, or other text emphasis formatting in newsletter items.
Do not put quotation marks around event names in headlines. Exception: when the headline names a composition such as a film, play or book, quote it per the composition-title rule.
Use single quotation marks for titles of works (books, films, etc.) in headlines.
Use double quotation marks for titles of works (books, films, etc.) in body text.
Do not italicize titles of works. Use quotation marks instead per the headline and body rules.
Do not use the Oxford comma (serial comma). In a list of three or more, omit the comma before 'and' or 'or'. Example: 'red, white and blue' not 'red, white, and blue'.
Hyphenate compound modifiers before a noun. Example: 'full-time employee' not 'full time employee'.
Use 'in' for rooms and buildings when describing event locations. Example: '3-4 p.m. Tuesday, Feb. 10, in TLC 245'.
Capitalize academic terms (Fall, Spring, Summer) only when a year follows. Example: 'Fall 2026' but 'this fall'.
Use Q&A formatting when the submission references a question-and-answer format.

Pair the correct day of the week with every date that falls within the next 30 days, based on the applicable calendar year. This applies to event dates, deadlines, registration deadlines, application deadlines, enrollment deadlines, submission deadlines, drawing dates, promotional dates and every other date reference. Scan the entire submission before finalizing so non-event dates are not overlooked. Dates beyond 30 days do not need a day of the week.

Never guess or silently correct a date. When a supplied weekday and date do not match, keep both exactly as written and add a flag stating the correct weekday for the date given, for example: DATE CONFLICT: MARCH 3, 2027, IS A WEDNESDAY, NOT A TUESDAY. When the same event has different dates in the headline, body, links or notes, keep the body date and add a flag naming the other date, for example: DATE CONFLICT: HEADLINE SAYS MARCH 4. When a date has no year, assume the next upcoming occurrence after the submission date. When adding a missing weekday, calculate it from the calendar for that resolved year, never from today's date or the publication date. If the weekday cannot be verified, add the flag DAY OF WEEK NOT VERIFIED instead of adding a weekday. Report these conflicts in the flags list for the editor; do not write them into the headline or body.
Events are assumed to be free unless otherwise noted. If an event has a cost, include the price. Do not write 'free' unless the original submission explicitly states it.
Do not include the year for events occurring within 12 months of the publication date, even if the event is in the next calendar year. Include the year only for events more than 12 months out.
Abbreviate 'University of Idaho' to 'U of I' on all references. Do not write out 'University of Idaho' repeatedly. Never use 'UI' alone as an abbreviation.

Start event-detail constructions with the time, then give the day, date and location in that order. Example: '3-4 p.m. Wednesday, Feb. 12, in the Pitman Center Vandal Ballroom.' Never place the day or date before the time. Keep the time, day, date and location in the same complete sentence as the event name. Never begin a separate sentence with a time, date, day of the week or location fragment. Correct: 'Stop by the Asian Studies Library Open House 2-4 p.m. Thursday, Sept. 3, in Admin 204.' Incorrect: 'Stop by the Asian Studies Library Open House. 2-4 p.m. Thursday, Sept. 3, in Admin 204.' Do not omit these elements. If the event is more than one month away, omit the day of the week.
Always write 'Vandal Gear' as two capitalized words. Replace 'VandalGear', 'Vandal gear' or other variants with 'Vandal Gear'.
Do not include 'PT' or 'Pacific time' unless the event is in another time zone such as Boise, Twin Falls or Idaho Falls. All events are assumed Pacific time by default.
Use em dashes — with spaces on both sides. Replace all en dashes with em dashes.
Format phone numbers as XXX-XXX-XXXX. Do not use parentheses around the area code.

Apply these acronym checks in order. 1. Inside an official name: an acronym that is part of an official event, program, product, website or organization name stays exactly as submitted, with no expansion and no parenthetical. 2. Never-spell-out list: IMCI, IRIC, COBRE, INBRE, EPSCoR and ISUB always stand alone, even on first reference, with no expansion and no parenthetical. 3. Widely known acronyms: following AP style, use acronyms such as AI, GPS, FBI and NASA without spelling them out. U of I is also exempt. 4. Everything else: spell out the full name on first reference in the body. Add the acronym in parentheses after the full name only when the acronym appears again later in the body or in the headline, then use only the acronym. If the acronym is not used again, write the full name alone and leave the acronym out. No acronym may appear before that definition, except under checks 1 through 3. An acronym may appear in a headline only when the body defines it on first reference or it passes check 1, 2 or 3. When unsure whether an acronym is widely known, spell it out on first reference.
Flag language that could reasonably be read as Diversity, Equity and Inclusion-related for editor review, even if it may ultimately be acceptable.

NEVER add information, facts, names, URLs, or references that are not present in the original submission, except approved canonical expansions or addresses supplied by an active style rule, or the standard full name of an acronym when the acronym rule requires a first-reference definition. When you supply an acronym's full name that is not in the submitted text, add a warning flag naming spell_out_acronyms so an editor can verify the expansion. Every remaining detail in the edited version must be traceable to the submitted text. Do not merge or cross-reference content from other submissions.

When embedding a hyperlink, do not repeat the anchor text in the surrounding sentence. Integrate the link so the anchor text appears exactly once. Example: write 'and online' not 'and online via online'.
Capitalize proper names, event titles, and program names in both headlines and body text. Example: 'Pizza & the Past' not 'pizza & the past'. This applies even in sentence-case headlines.
Use the word 'online' instead of platform names like 'Zoom', 'Teams', or 'Webex' when describing virtual attendance options, unless the platform name is essential (e.g., a Teams-specific training).

Use short, complete sentences. Each sentence should communicate one main idea. Do not use semicolons. Replace semicolons with periods. Split compound or lengthy sentences into separate sentences. Favor clear, direct wording over complex sentence structures. Keep sentences concise and easy to read. Never separate an event from its time, date or location when shortening or splitting prose; keep those details together in one complete sentence.

Research recruitment announcements must begin with the most specific accurate audience description supplied by the source, followed by the study topic. Never default to generic words such as 'participants,' 'individuals' or 'people' when the source identifies breastfeeding or lactating women, donors, volunteers, faculty members, first-year students, alumni or another precise group. Include important eligibility qualifiers, such as an age range, in the first sentence whenever concise. Example: 'Researchers are seeking breastfeeding women ages 18-50 for a study on human milk composition,' not 'Researchers are recruiting participants for a study.' Follow with compensation and participation details.

Headlines must be written from the reader's perspective using verbs that accurately reflect the action the original submission asks readers to take. Preserve the primary action, purpose and intent; never substitute a different activity or transaction. When an author reads from a book, invite readers to hear the reading, not read or purchase the book. Correct: 'Hear Elizabeth Bradfield read from SOFAR'. Incorrect: 'Read Elizabeth Bradfield's poetry collection SOFAR' and 'Purchase Elizabeth Bradfield's poetry collection'. Likewise, write 'Participate in a VR research study', not 'Recruit research participants'.
Always spell out the name of a state. Example: 'Moscow, Idaho' not 'Moscow, ID'.

Replace '&' with 'and' everywhere in published plain text, including official names, titles, departments, programs and event names, except Q&A. HTML entities used by markup are not editorial ampersands.

Do not change the wording or capitalization of event titles. Keep event titles in title case exactly as submitted, even when the surrounding text uses sentence case. This applies everywhere the name appears, including inside sentence-case headlines: official event, program and organization names are proper nouns, and preserving their official capitalization takes precedence over sentence-casing. Example: 'Fraternity and Sorority Life Bid Day' stays fully capitalized inside an otherwise sentence-case headline, never 'fraternity and sorority Bid Day'. The ampersand rule is the sole wording exception: replace '&' with 'and' while preserving all other title wording and capitalization. When an event title is itself a composition title, such as a film, play or lecture title, format it under the composition-title rule instead.
If the submission includes 'Mountain time', retain it exactly as written. If 'MDT' or 'MST' appears, replace it with 'Mountain time'. Do not omit, rephrase or alter this wording.
When an address includes a directional abbreviation (N, S, E or W), add a period after the letter. Example: '1000 W. Pullman Road'. Do not leave directional abbreviations without a period.

Structure announcements around one clear call to action and supporting context. Replace vague instructions with an explicit action, but do not repeat that action elsewhere in the item. Use direct information-first contact language such as 'For more information, contact Betsy Church,' never 'Interested participants should contact Betsy Church.' Edit user-supplied linked text when needed for clarity, concision and editorial style; linked text is not immutable. Replace generic unlinked references such as 'landing page,' 'webpage,' 'here' or 'click here' with descriptive linked text that names the action or destination. Do not introduce audience qualifiers that are not in the original submission. When the submission provides a contact's full name, use it rather than a bare email address. Link the action verb or object: 'Sign up', 'Register for the workshop', 'Apply for the scholarship' or 'Review the promotion details'.

Promotional announcements must lead with the action readers should take and the benefit they can receive. Put important qualifying details early when they define the offer. Avoid passive, circular or redundant introductions such as 'The last week to have a permit reimbursed is this week.' Prefer 'This is the final week to enroll in a qualifying meal plan for a chance to have a commuter parking permit reimbursed in full.' Remove audience references that do not affect eligibility. Consolidate repeated actions into one descriptive linked call to action and shorten supporting wording rather than repeating the offer. For event items, the item sentence order rule decides where the call to action goes, and headlines follow the headline rules.

When the original submission provides an email address for a contact person or unit, hyperlink the person's or unit's name with that email address instead of displaying the address as plain text. Keep phone numbers from the original submission. Never repeat the contact's name in place of contact information: write 'contact Paul Rowley' (name linked) or 'contact Paul Rowley at 208-885-1234', never 'contact Paul Rowley at Paul Rowley' or 'contact Paul Rowley at prowley@uidaho.edu'. In a contact line, 'at' must be followed by meaningful information such as a phone number or location. If no email address or phone number is provided, use the name alone.

Preserve every deadline, actionable date and mandatory requirement from the original submission: registration, application, abstract, proposal, nomination and submission deadlines; event dates and times; application periods; eligibility, age and enrollment conditions; regulatory requirements; and required licenses or certifications. Keep mandatory language mandatory and never shorten a requirement until it appears optional or less important. Keep multiple deadlines when they serve different purposes. Never replace a specific deadline with a generic call to action such as 'Learn more and register'. When editing for conciseness, shorten the surrounding prose instead of removing deadlines or requirements. Example: 'Registration closes Oct. 23. Abstract submissions are due Oct. 16. Applicants must be TIPS certified. Learn more and register.' is correct; dropping any deadline or requirement is not.

Preserve the specific organization that grants, administers or oversees an award, ranking, rating, certification, accreditation, recognition or designation. Also preserve the university program, office, department or initiative that offers, sponsors or administers an opportunity, service, event, grant, program or activity. When that entity is central to understanding the opportunity, name it early in the body; retaining it only in the headline is not sufficient. Shorten surrounding wording, not the identity or role of the awarding or sponsoring entity. Example: keep 'Association for Advancement in Sustainability in Higher Education STARS Gold-rated university,' not only 'STARS Gold-rated university,' and keep 'raise funds through Idaho Eats,' not only 'raise funds.'

Preserve every distinct action and information-seeking option offered by the source. If readers may sign up or learn more, retain both options; do not narrow a general invitation to contact or reach out into registration-only language unless registration is the source's sole purpose. A request for more information is not a duplicate call to action and takes precedence over the single-CTA rule. Shorten surrounding wording instead of deleting the information path.

The headline must not begin with the same wording as the first sentence of the body, and must not be the first sentence or a minor rewording of it. It may mention the same event, name or date. Example: for a body opening 'The Example Center will hold its pottery sale 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Saturday, Dec. 5, in the Example Hall.', write 'Buy handmade pottery at the Example Center sale', not 'The Example Center will hold its pottery sale'.

When condensing, distinguish unnecessary repetition from meaningful context. Preserve participant responsibilities and operational details explaining what volunteers, attendees or other participants will actually do. Also preserve traditions and ceremonies, participant activities, routes, locations and event logistics, notable event features, and details that help readers visualize or understand the event or opportunity. Achieve conciseness by tightening wording, not by deleting these details. Example: 'Sororities will open bids at 11:15 a.m. and run home to their chapters down Idaho Avenue.' is correct; shortening it to 'Sororities will open bids at 11:15 a.m.' removes meaningful participant activity and is not.
Each call to action must appear only once. Do not repeat action verbs or equivalent CTA phrases before or after a link. If one CTA accomplishes the goal, do not add another with the same meaning.

Do not narrow, broaden or genericize the intended audience, and never invent it. Newsletter channel context such as TDR faculty and staff or My UI students is distribution metadata, never source content, so do not add an audience group from the selected newsletter. A submission sent to both newsletters must remain audience-neutral unless its source explicitly names a group. Preserve broad audience meaning such as 'all are welcome,' 'everyone is invited' or 'the public is welcome.' Also preserve the most specific accurate source description, such as donors, breastfeeding or lactating women, volunteers, faculty members, first-year students or alumni, instead of replacing it with 'participants,' 'individuals' or 'people.' For recruitment announcements, include the specific group in the first sentence whenever possible and surface important eligibility qualifiers early enough that the offer is not misleading. For concise event invitations, replace broad wording with a direct invitation such as 'Attend the workshop,' never with a narrower group unless the original explicitly limits attendance.

Apply AP title capitalization to composition titles. Use single quotation marks in headlines and double quotation marks in body text for books, films, plays, poems, albums, songs, operas, programs, lectures, speeches and works of art. Do not quote holy books, reference works, software, apps, game titles or sculptures. Preserve consistent quotation and capitalization throughout the item. When an event is named for a composition — a film screening, play, reading, lecture or similar work — this rule governs the title's quotation marks and capitalization and takes precedence over event-title preservation and the ban on quoting event names in headlines.

For on-campus locations, place the building name first, followed by the room or venue with no comma between them. Never format a location as Room, Building. Examples: ISUB Reflections Gallery, Bruce M. Pitman Center International Ballroom and IRIC 352.

When an approved off-campus venue appears, append its canonical address exactly: Kenworthy Performing Arts Centre, 508 S. Main St.; 1912 Center, 412 E. Third St.; One World Cafe, 840 W. Seventh St.; Hunga Dunga Brewing Co., 333 N. Jackson St.; Moscow Public Library, 110 S. Jefferson St.; Palouse-Clearwater Environmental Institute, 1040 Rodeo Drive; Best Western Plus University Inn, 1516 W. Pullman Road; East City Park, 900 E. Third St. Add addresses only for venues on this list.

Preserve the purpose, value and context that explain why an event, service or opportunity is offered. Preserve contact information and every official contact title supplied by the source; never remove a title solely for brevity. Capitalize a title immediately before a person's name. Prefer placing it after the name in AP-style lowercase, such as 'Danny Conklin, concessions manager,' and keep each title associated with the correct person. Shorten wording, not meaning or credentials.

Tighten wording only when it makes the item clearer and the meaning stays exactly the same. Do not rewrite a sentence that is already clear and concise just because another phrasing is possible; leave it as submitted apart from changes another active rule requires. Correct obvious spelling, capitalization and typographical errors, except inside protected names. Concise possessives and similar tightening fall under this rule, not separate requirements.

Keep these exactly as submitted, with no expanding, shortening, recapitalizing or correcting: website, platform and product names; event names, including any acronyms inside them; names of people, including spelling and middle initials; and titles of classes, guides, articles and podcasts. Titles of classes, guides, articles and podcasts still take the quotation marks the composition-title rule requires, but their words and capitalization stay as submitted. Replacing '&' with 'and' under the ampersand rule is the only wording exception. If a protected name looks misspelled or appears in more than one form, use the most complete submitted form and add a warning flag whose message is '[NAME VARIES IN SUBMISSION: CONFIRM OFFICIAL NAME]'. Venues, buildings and organizations: when a submitted name matches a canonical form supplied by an active rule, use that form; otherwise keep the submitted name. Never create a new capitalized venue name, and never add words such as 'Office', 'Department' or 'Center' to an organization's name. If a venue is unclear, keep it as submitted and add a warning flag whose message is '[CONFIRM VENUE NAME]'.

Default sentence order for event items: 1. who, what, time, day, date and place; 2. brief background with one credential; 3. the main call to action; 4. secondary events. When that order makes a sentence awkward, a natural sentence wins within these limits: event details stay in the first or second sentence; an overloaded opening splits into two complete sentences; background may move later or be cut but never comes before the event details; the call to action may move up, for example when the item is mainly about registering, as long as the event details stay near the top. For notices that are not events, such as closures, deadline changes and other updates, lead with the current facts, then mention the earlier plan only if needed, then the call to action. The time, day, date and place order inside the event details never changes.

Trim a long quotation from an outside source to the part that supports the item, unless the submitter notes ask to keep it. Trimming must not remove facts, deadlines, requirements or the action readers should take. Do not flag a quotation you trimmed.

Every headline follows these rules. 1. Ask readers to act: start with a verb naming the specific action tied to the main call to action. 'Buy tickets', 'Register' and 'Submit' beat vague verbs such as 'Attend' when a more specific action applies. 2. Write a complete phrase, with articles and connecting words: 'Get tickets to see the Example Quartet in concert', not 'Attend Example Quartet performance'. 3. Do not begin the headline with the same wording as the first sentence of the body; it may mention the same event, name or date. 4. Use sentence case. 5. Never use exclamation marks.

Use curly quotation marks and apostrophes (‘ ’ “ ”) in headlines and body text. Never convert curly marks to straight ones, and convert straight marks from the submission to curly ones. Leave URLs and HTML attributes unchanged.

Write calls to action in the active voice, addressed to the reader: 'Register by Friday', not 'Registration should be completed by Friday'. Use 'can', not 'may', for what readers are able to do: 'Employees can enroll online', not 'Employees may enroll online'. Keep 'may' only where it means permission or possibility.
With a compound verb, place the adverb before the helping verb, following AP style ('also will give', not 'will also give'), unless that changes the meaning or reads awkwardly.
Do not repeat a distinctive word or phrase in nearby sentences. Repeating names, places and basic terms is fine when clarity requires it.

Never put review notes, bracketed flags or questions for staff in the headline or body. Report each one in the flags list instead, with the bracketed note as the flag message, for example '[CONFIRM VENUE NAME]' or '[DATE CONFLICT: MARCH 3, 2027, IS A WEDNESDAY, NOT A TUESDAY]'. Keep the source wording in the copy where the note applies.
